extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical Euclidean geometry (readers of Euclid-like propositions)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted propositions and construction rules from a classical Euclidean-style text concerning areas, rectangles/squares, proportionality, and geometric (algebraic) identities, plus methods to determine unknown sides from given data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a triangle as half the product of base and height
rubrics_metrics.description: «l'area del triangolo viene della multiplicarione della linea [base] per la metà della linea [altezza]» — the area of a triangle is obtained by multiplying the base by half the corresponding altitude (height).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by constructing a rectangle on the base whose one side equals the altitude; the triangle's area equals half that rectangle. The text gives constructions and numeric examples showing how multiplying a base by the half of the perpendicular yields the triangle area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a right triangle equals half the product of the legs (catheti)
rubrics_metrics.description: «larea di' quello triangolo fa da multiplicare la mita del catetto ...» — For a right triangle, its area equals one-half the product of its two perpendicular sides (the catheti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly in proofs: form the rectangle whose sides are the two legs, and take half of its area. The text uses examples and numerical computations to illustrate (showing the rectangle area then halving it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles that stand on the same base and are between the same parallel lines have equal areas (i.e., equal base and equal altitude ⇒ equal area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used as a basic equivalence: when triangles share base and altitude (or lie between the same parallels), their areas are interchangeable in constructions and proportionality arguments. The text applies this to reduce area-computation problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric multiplication of line segments produces rectangle area
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying two line segments is represented geometrically by the rectangle with those segments as adjacent sides; the product (multiplication) corresponds to the rectangle's area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book repeatedly replaces algebraic products by rectangles: to 'multiply' a·b construct rectangle with sides a and b. This underlies many constructions and numeric examples where products of lengths are compared to triangle areas or squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square (potentia) of a line equals area of square constructed on that line
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'potentia' (square) of a line is represented by the area of the square constructed on that line; squares of lines are compared and combined to represent algebraic squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in identities and comparisons (e.g., comparing sums/differences of squares with rectangles). The text uses 'potentia' to denote geometrical square and manipulates them via constructions and proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric identity for square of a sum: (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2
rubrics_metrics.description: The square on the sum of two line segments equals the sum of the squares on the parts together with twice the rectangle contained by the parts — expressed geometrically by decomposing a big square into smaller squares and rectangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates this by dividing a square on (a+b) into the square on a, square on b, and two equal rectangles each of area a·b; numeric examples are provided to illustrate the decomposition and the resulting areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric identity for square of a difference (and related difference-of-squares relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: The square on the difference of two segments and various difference-of-squares relations are expressed geometrically: differences of squares can be represented as rectangles involving sum and difference of the segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to transform problems about unknown segments into geometric areas/rectangles: e.g., square(whole) − square(part) = rectangle(sum, difference). The text gives constructive steps and numeric demonstrations to find these relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-scaling: area of similar/composed figures scales with products of line factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When segments or figures are multiplied or combined, the resulting area changes according to multiplication of the corresponding linear measures; e.g., multiplying a side by a factor multiplies corresponding rectangle/square areas by that factor (and squares by factor^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows how repeating or scaling line segments (adding multiples, taking halves) affects the area: e.g., multiplying a line by n multiplies the square on it by n^2 and the rectangle by n. Several worked numeric cases illustrate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to find unknown side(s) from given side(s) and area using perpendiculars and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given one side of a triangle and the area (and sometimes another side or proportional data), construct perpendiculars and use rectangle/square relations and proportions to determine unknown side lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text outlines methods: place the known side, drop a perpendicular from an appropriate point, form rectangles whose areas correspond to given quantities, and use multiplication/division (geometric products) and taking square roots (constructing the square root via geometric means) to find the unknown length. Worked numerical examples illustrate the step-by-step method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of triangle-area problems by decomposing into rectangles and known parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Many area problems are solved by decomposing triangles and related figures into rectangles, squares, and halves thereof, so the unknown area or side can be obtained from known rectangular areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly builds auxiliary squares/rectangles and uses equalities of areas (e.g., halves, sums) to convert triangle-area computations into rectangle multiplications, enabling solutions via geometric 'algebra'. This includes practical guidance on where to draw perpendiculars and how to partition figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of triangles by side/angle correspondences and transfer of equalities via parallels/perpendiculars
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles with corresponding sides and angles equal (or placed by equal parallels/perpendiculars) are equal in area and can be substituted for each other in constructions and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify replacing one triangle by another in area computations and proportionality chains; the text details building equalities by dropping parallels/perpendiculars and pairing corresponding sides to derive equal areas.
